title: Nachmanides' other way
hookLine: a more mystical approach to the same texts

cards: A hot afternoon. Abraham sits at the opening of his tent, looks up, and sees three men standing nearby. He runs to meet them, bows, and hurries Sarah to bake bread while he picks out a calf.
A homely scene from Genesis. Now hand it to two great rabbis named Moses. One says it all happened in a prophetic vision.
The other says those words contradict Scripture. Same text, same tent, two very different readings.

teach.b: Nachmanides' other way. His name was Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, known as the Ramban, from Girona, in Catalonia. First, he argues out loud.
In the Guide, Maimonides reads the three men as something Abraham saw in a prophetic vision.

In his commentary on Genesis, the Ramban quotes him, then pushes back hard: these words, he says, contradict Scripture, and one shouldn't listen to them. If it was only a vision, why the bread, the calf, the hurrying?
He reads the visitors as real messengers, seen in a form people could see. Second, the offerings.
Maimonides explains the sacrifices as a gentle step: people in the ancient world knew worship by offerings, so the Torah kept the form and turned it toward God alone. The Ramban objects.

teach.h: A SWEET SAVOUR UNTO THE LORD.
teach.b: The Torah calls an offering "of a sweet savour unto the LORD."
He sees in it a picture for the one who brings it: what is done to the animal should make the person think, this should have been me, and the offering stands in their place.
Third, the way of truth. The Ramban drops a short hint and says the meaning is known by the way of truth, pointing to a hidden, mystical layer of the Torah, the tradition known as Kabbalah. He hints.

Maimonides reaches for reason and philosophy; the Ramban, for the plain story and for hidden depths. Both read the same verses seriously. Students still open both, side by side, and learn from the argument.

how: The Ramban's Torah commentary is printed in standard rabbinic Bibles, and students often read it alongside other commentators, comparing how each one reads the same verse.

games.q: you're the Ramban, and Maimonides has written that Abraham's three visitors came in a prophetic vision. what do you do?

games.why: he quotes the Guide and pushes back hard. yet both men's books are still read side by side.

practice: Pick one question that matters to you, like why people suffer or why pray, and give it two readers: one who answers with careful reasons, step by step, and one who answers with a story, or a sense that something deeper is hidden there.
Let each speak for a few breaths without interrupting. You don't have to choose a winner; just notice what each one sees that the other misses.

wordCard.voice: Nachmanides' other way. The Ramban's reading of the Torah: close to the plain story, open to a hidden way of truth, and willing to argue with Maimonides by name. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the way of truth, the Ramban's phrase for a hidden, mystical meaning of a verse.

carryVoice: Your line: two ways of thinking. One Torah can hold both readers. Back tomorrow, same hill.
